title: The Arsenal and the Statehouse: New Defense Firms, Venture Capital and State Industrial Policy
gist: Venture-backed defense entrants like Anduril, Saronic, and Regent are now using state economic development subsidies — $830 million from Ohio for Anduril's Arsenal-1 alone — as the bridge across the valley of death between VC rounds and federal programs of record; Alley argues this hands statehouses a fiscal stake that will politically protect failing programs and make the most dynamic part of the defense industrial base as rigid as the primes.

themes.theme: State Subsidies as the New Defense Capital Stack

insights.claim: Anduril received $830 million in incentives from Ohio for its Arsenal-1 drone plant — a $310 million grant, $452 million in tax credits, and roughly $70 million in site and airport financing — against a $910 million announced facility cost.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: State money covered nearly the entire announced facility cost — model new defense entrants' capex as substantially state-funded, which flatters their capital efficiency versus primes.
insights.quote: Anduril received $830 million in incentives from Ohio, including a $310 million grant, $452 million in tax credits, and roughly $70 million in site and airport financing.
insights.locator: New defense firms can draw on state subsidies

insights.claim: Anduril sited Arsenal-1 near Columbus partially because of state subsidies rather than congressional allocation, inverting the traditional geography of defense production.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Plant location is now a competitive state-bidding outcome — track statehouse incentive packages, not appropriations earmarks, to anticipate where defense capacity lands.
insights.quote: Anduril sited Arsenal-1 near Columbus partially because of state subsidies.
insights.locator: When Anduril announced a $910 million drone production facility

insights.claim: The political tell for this shift is that Representative Mike Carey's press release thanked Governor Mike DeWine rather than claiming credit himself — a member of Congress could not claim credit for defense jobs he did not deliver.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Credit-claiming behavior is a leading indicator of where procurement power actually sits; watch governors' press releases as a new signal channel.
insights.quote: Members of Congress usually take substantial credit for defense industrial jobs, but Carey did not because he could not.
insights.locator: When Anduril announced a $910 million drone production facility

insights.claim: Saronic took $5 million in grants plus workforce assistance from Louisiana to expand a shipyard in Franklin, and Regent will receive up to $13 million from Rhode Island contingent on hitting employment targets.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: The subsidy playbook has spread well beyond Anduril and into maritime autonomy and sea gliders — expect every scaling defense startup to have a statehouse counterparty.
insights.quote: Saronic, a company that builds unmanned and autonomous vessels, likewise took $5 million in grants and additional workforce assistance from Louisiana to expand a shipyard in Franklin.
insights.locator: New defense firms can draw on state subsidies

insights.claim: State subsidies function as risk transfer, making new firms more likely to recoup startup costs and their venture backers more likely to recoup their investments.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: State grants effectively de-risk the VC position in defense tech — a hidden subsidy to venture returns that should be priced into defense-tech valuations.
insights.quote: These make firms more likely to recoup their startup costs, and their venture backers more likely to recoup their investments.
insights.locator: State economic development funds make scaling defense production

themes.theme: Venture Economics vs. Programs of Record

insights.claim: Around 75 percent of venture-backed startups that raise at least $1 million never return investors' capital, and only roughly 4 percent return 10 times or more — so most new defense entrants are statistically doomed to fail.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Apply venture base rates to the defense-tech cohort: the modal outcome for any named new entrant is capital loss, regardless of sector narrative.
insights.quote: Around 75 percent of venture-backed startups that raise at least $1 million do not return investors’ capital.
insights.locator: Venture firms make these investments and expect to profit

insights.claim: New defense entrants invert the traditional procurement sequence: they use venture money to prototype capability first and then offer it to the Department of Defense, building capacity ahead of programs of record rather than in response to federal requirements.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: This is a build-first, sell-later model — revenue visibility is far worse than primes', so treat new entrants as pre-revenue industrials, not defense contractors.
insights.quote: This builds capacity ahead of programs of record, and bets that demonstrated prototypes and production will win stable contracts.
insights.locator: Venture Capital, Defense Allocations and New Business Models

insights.claim: The gap between intermittent other-transaction funding and a stable program of record is a well-known 'valley of death' where many defense firms cannot sustain operations.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Program-of-record conversion is the single binary event that determines a defense startup's survival — everything before it is bridge financing.
insights.quote: The gap between less consistent funding from other transactions and programs of record is a well-known valley of death where many firms cannot sustain operations.
insights.locator: This has several consequences for defense firms

insights.claim: Firms living on other-transaction agreements live contract-to-contract in the same way they live funding-round-to-funding-round, stacking two independent sources of financing fragility.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Compounding contract risk with funding-round risk means correlated blowups — a VC funding winter and a contract lapse would hit the same names simultaneously.
insights.quote: Other transactions or similar agreements can have firms living from contract to contract in the same way they live from funding round to funding round.
insights.locator: Unlike with the traditional process the primes follow

insights.claim: For established primes, subsidies do not change where or what they build, because they follow programs of record whose location is set by congressional appropriations, talent clusters, and political considerations.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Do not read state incentive competition as a signal for prime contractors — the mechanism is specific to pre-program-of-record entrants.
insights.quote: For most firms like the primes, subsidies do not change where or what they build.
insights.locator: While states have long offered subsidies to defense contractors

insights.claim: Lockheed Martin's 2017 move of F-16 production to Greenville, South Carolina illustrates the old model: no real site competition, only $1.5 million in state grants, with Senator Lindsey Graham claiming credit via foreign military sales to Bahrain and others that kept the line open.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: The $1.5 million versus $830 million contrast quantifies how much more state capital new entrants extract than primes — a structural cost advantage for challengers.
insights.quote: South Carolina’s governor had a more peripheral role, enabling $1.5 million in grants for building improvements.
insights.locator: Lockheed Martin’s 2017 decision to move F-16 production

insights.claim: Coalitions of congressmen, statehouses, firms, and workers may politically protect new defense entrants even when their unproven capabilities fail, saddling the defense budget with programs that promised innovation but did not deliver.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: The failure mode for defense-tech is not clean bankruptcy but zombie programs — expect revenue floors for subsidized firms and budget drag on the DoD topline.
insights.quote: Political coalitions of Congressmen, statehouses, firms, and workers may protect new entrants politically even if unproven capabilities fail.
insights.locator: New defense firms backed by venture financing

insights.claim: State politics could make the most dynamic part of the defense industry more rigid by importing the same political problems that bedevil legacy programs — the central contrarian claim against the defense-tech innovation narrative.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: The bull case for defense tech rests on dynamism; if state capture ossifies it, multiples built on 'not-a-prime' premia are mispriced.
insights.quote: State politics might thus make the most dynamic part of the defense industry more rigid by introducing the political problems that bedevil some existing programs.
insights.locator: Political coalitions of Congressmen, statehouses, firms

insights.claim: Congress will fight hard to keep production and maintenance lines open in their constituencies even when the armed services themselves do not want the system.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Service-level program cancellations are weak signals — congressional district exposure is the better predictor of whether a line actually closes.
insights.quote: Congress will often fight hard to keep production and maintenance lines open in their constituencies, even if the services themselves don’t want the system.
insights.locator: State subsidies also engage Congress

insights.claim: Procurement rigidity produces distortions that even huge increases in defense spending cannot solve, such as foreign military sales that diverge from national interests.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: A rising defense topline does not fix allocation quality — spending growth may flow to subsidized rather than superior capabilities.
insights.quote: Such procurement rigidity causes problems that even huge increases in defense spending cannot solve, such as foreign military sales that diverge from national interests.
insights.locator: Giving state governments a significant fiscal stake

insights.claim: When new firms fail to deliver, states must choose between clawing back subsidies or eating sunk costs — and governments are usually reticent or unable to withdraw grants, as Ohio learned with Lordstown Motors' 2023 bankruptcy despite large state subsidies.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Clawback provisions are largely theoretical — state taxpayer losses on failed defense entrants are the realistic outcome, a fiscal and political risk at the state level.
insights.quote: Ohio faced this choice in a different industry with Lordstown Motors in 2023, which went bankrupt despite large state subsidies.
insights.locator: When new firms do not deliver what the military needs

insights.claim: A majority of the jobs promised at Anduril's Arsenal-1 might not be new employment, undercutting the economic development case states used to justify the incentives.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Job-creation headlines attached to defense plant announcements should be discounted heavily — the local economic benefit may not offset forgone tax revenue.
insights.quote: In the case of Arsenal-1, a majority of the promised jobs might not be new employment.
insights.locator: Last, these changes expose state and local taxpayers

insights.claim: States have shifted economic development work to privatized entities with weaker disclosure requirements — Texas negotiates through a 501(c)(3), the Texas Economic Development Corporation, with minimal financial disclosure before the state agency finalizes deals.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Deal terms for defense plant siting are becoming unobservable in public records — a genuine information asymmetry favoring insiders over public-market analysts.
insights.quote: For example, Texas uses a 501(c)(3) entity, the Texas Economic Development Corporation, to negotiate with minimal financial disclosure before the state agency finalizes deals.
insights.locator: States have also transferred much of their economic development work

insights.claim: Privatized state development corporations like JobsOhio are not subject to the public records requirements that congressional appropriations committees satisfy, making the fastest-growing channel of defense industrial funding the least transparent one.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Congressional appropriations data no longer captures the full defense industrial money flow — analysts relying on federal budget documents will miss state-level commitments.
insights.quote: Privatized state development corporations like JobsOhio are not subject to the same public records requirements.
insights.locator: Second, the rise of state subsidies reduces transparency

insights.claim: Conflicts of interest are already surfacing: Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has been criticized for venture capital ties to Anduril and potential conflicts with Arsenal-1, and Texas competition for a Saronic facility has produced disputes in Cameron County over tax abatements.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Political conflict-of-interest headlines are an emerging idiosyncratic risk for defense-tech names tied to specific statehouse patrons.
insights.quote: In Ohio, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy has received criticism for venture capital ties to Anduril and potential conflicts of interest with Arsenal-1.
insights.locator: Second, the rise of state subsidies reduces transparency

insights.claim: Venture firms are much larger political donors and lobbyists than the defense companies they back, and their political efforts have recently been accused of influencing procurement decisions.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Track VC lobbying disclosures, not portfolio-company ones, to anticipate acquisition policy shifts — the influence sits one layer up the capital stack.
insights.quote: Venture firms are much larger donors and lobbyists than the companies they back, and their political efforts have recently been accused of influencing procurement decisions.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, In Washington

insights.claim: There is little open-records evidence that new defense firms make significant state political donations to win subsidies — competition between states and their active economic development bodies makes donations unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: The corruption story here is not bribery but a state-versus-state race to the bottom; the winning state may end up worse off than the loser.
insights.quote: Political donations are not needed to win subsidies given competition between states and their active economic development bodies.
insights.locator: This ecosystem of funders and their lobbying

insights.claim: State-to-federal political pipelines compound the lock-in: Ohio Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted, in office at the time of Arsenal-1, was appointed to fill J.D. Vance's Senate seat and then highlighted his role funding the Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: State subsidy champions graduate into federal appropriators — a mechanism converting state incentives into durable federal funding for the same programs.
insights.quote: Once in the Senate, Husted followed the legislative textbook and highlighted his efforts in helping fund the Collaborative Combat Aircraft, knowing that voters reward such credit-claiming.
insights.locator: The result mixes standard Washington politics

themes.theme: Proposed Fixes: Subsidy Marketplace, Disclosure, Defense BRAC

insights.claim: Alley proposes the Department of Commerce organize a marketplace where states make incentive bids for defense firms, with Congress enforcing participation for firms seeking substantial federal funds via the Spending Clause.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: A federal subsidy auction would compress the state incentive premium new entrants currently capture — a policy risk to defense-tech capital efficiency.
insights.quote: First, the Department of Commerce could organize a marketplace where states make incentive bids for defense firms.
insights.locator: Three policy changes could help mitigate

insights.claim: Alley calls for a Base Realignment and Closure-style all-or-nothing review mechanism applied to defense programs protected by state subsidies, noting the BRAC delegation model already produced five rounds of reductions.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: A defense-program BRAC is the only credible kill mechanism proposed — its absence means assume subsidized programs persist indefinitely.
insights.quote: Third, Congress could follow principles from the Base Realignment and Closure Act, allowing an all-or-nothing review of programs that are not adding value, especially when state subsidies are in play.
insights.locator: Three policy changes could help mitigate

insights.claim: Open-records requirements should be extended to state private development corporations whenever the firms they court take federal funds, in any sector — not just defense.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: If enacted, this would create a new public dataset on state incentive packages — a future analytical edge for tracking industrial policy flows.
insights.quote: Second, Congress should enforce open-records requirements for state private development corporations when firms take federal funds regardless of sector.
insights.locator: Three policy changes could help mitigate

insights.claim: Alley concedes new firms are not wrong to take state subsidies, since refusing would be a competitive disadvantage — the problem is systemic incentive design, not firm-level behavior.
insights.speaker: Joshua Alley
insights.so_what: Expect universal adoption of the subsidy playbook across the sector; any firm forgoing it is structurally disadvantaged on cost.
insights.quote: To be clear, new firms are not wrong to take state subsidies when not doing so would put them at a competitive disadvantage.
insights.locator: To be clear, new firms are not wrong
